_meta.description: Endgame theory tree - Position → Try → Teach format. One lesson = one idea, multiple positions reinforcing the same concept.
_meta.structure: Categories → Lessons → Positions. Each position: show → user tries → feedback + rule.

basic_mates.name: Basic Checkmates
basic_mates.description: Turn a winning queen or rook into checkmate without stalemating the king.

queen_mate.name: Mate with Queen
queen_mate.rule: Use the queen to make a smaller box, bring your king close, then place the queen one knight-move away from the enemy king for mate.
queen_mate.description: The queen makes the box smaller. Your king closes the last escape squares. Keep one legal square available until you are ready to mate.

positions.prompt: What queen move cuts the king down to the last two ranks?
positions.idea: Qd7 controls every square on the seventh rank. The black king is now held near the back edge while White's king approaches.
positions.on_correct: Qd7 makes the box smaller without stalemating the king. Now bring your king closer.
positions.on_wrong: A distant check makes the king move but does not organize the mate. First use the queen to build a clear wall.
positions.rule_reminder: Queen first: make a smaller box. King second: walk toward the box.

positions.prompt: The queen is doing its job. Which king move prepares the finish?
positions.idea: Kf6 brings White's king close enough to protect the queen on the mating rank. The queen does not need another check yet.
positions.on_correct: Kf6 brings the king into the finish. With both pieces working together, mate is close.
positions.on_wrong: Another queen check only sends the king around the box. Bring your king close so it can guard the queen.
positions.rule_reminder: Once the box is small, stop checking and bring your king.

positions.prompt: Finish the checkmate in one move.
positions.idea: Qg7 is protected by the king on f6. The queen checks h8 and controls g8 and h7, so every escape square is closed.
positions.on_correct: Qg7 is checkmate. The queen gives the check and your king protects the queen.
positions.on_wrong: That is only another check. Look for a queen square protected by your king that also covers every escape square.
positions.rule_reminder: For the finish, the queen checks and the king protects the queen.

rook_mate.name: Mate with Rook
rook_mate.rule: Use the rook as a wall, bring your king close, then check along the edge when your king controls the escape squares.
rook_mate.description: A rook cannot finish alone. It cuts off a rank or file while your king walks up to support the final check.

positions.prompt: Where should the rook build a wall around the king?
positions.idea: Ra7 controls the entire seventh rank. The black king stays on the back rank while White's king approaches.
positions.on_correct: Ra7 builds the wall. Keep the rook safe and bring your king closer next.
positions.on_wrong: A check makes the king move but does not improve your king. Build the wall first, then walk your king up.
positions.rule_reminder: Rook makes the wall. King walks toward the trapped king.

positions.prompt: The rook holds the wall. Which king move prepares mate?
positions.idea: Kf6 brings White's king close enough to control g7 and g8. The rook can then give the final edge check.
positions.on_correct: Kf6 joins the rook. The black king is now ready to be mated on the back rank.
positions.on_wrong: Checking too soon only sends the king along the edge. Bring your king close enough to control the escape squares.
positions.rule_reminder: Do not check forever. Bring the king until it controls the next rank.

positions.prompt: Finish the checkmate without stalemating Black.
positions.idea: Ra8 checks across the back rank and controls g8. White's king on g6 controls g7 and h7, so Black has no escape.
positions.on_correct: Ra8 is checkmate. The rook checks while your king removes the only escape squares.
positions.on_wrong: Rg7 closes every escape square without giving check, which is stalemate. When the king has no escape, your move must give check.
positions.rule_reminder: No escape plus no check is stalemate. Give the final rook check.

king_and_pawn.name: King & Pawn
king_and_pawn.description: The foundation of all endgames. Master king activity and pawn promotion.

opposition.name: Kings Face Off (Opposition)
opposition.rule: Put your King in front of the pawn. When the Kings face each other with one square between them, make the other King give way.
opposition.description: Chess players call this opposition: the Kings face each other with one empty square between them. Use that shape to lead your pawn forward.

positions.prompt: White to move. How do you make progress?
positions.idea: Step sideways with Kd5 so your King can get around the defender. Move the King while it can still advance; the pawn follows.
positions.on_correct: Exactly. Kd5 makes the Black King choose a side. Your King can now lead the pawn forward.
positions.on_wrong: Pushing e4 lets Black's King face yours and hold the draw. Your King must lead.
positions.rule_reminder: Put the King in front of the pawn. Let the pawn follow.

positions.prompt: Critical position. White to move. How do you win?
positions.idea: d6 lets Black build a drawing setup. Kf6 goes around the Black King and keeps it boxed in.
positions.on_correct: Perfect. Kf6 forces Black's King aside. After ...Ke8, Ke6 maintains full control.
positions.on_wrong: d6 lets Black reach a drawing setup after ...Kd7. Bring your King to the sixth rank before the pawn.
positions.rule_reminder: Bring your King to the sixth rank before pushing the pawn there.

positions.prompt: White to move. What's the right plan?
positions.idea: Advance the King, not the pawn. Kd5 makes the Kings face each other with one square between them, so Black must step aside.
positions.on_correct: Right. Kd5 makes Black give ground.
positions.on_wrong: e5 lets Black play ...Ke7 and build the same face-to-face drawing setup.
positions.rule_reminder: Advance the King first. The pawn advances last.

key_squares.name: The Squares Your King Needs
key_squares.rule: For a pawn near its starting square, aim your King for the three squares two ranks ahead. Reaching the right one lets the King lead the pawn through.
key_squares.description: Chess players call these key squares. They are the nearby target squares your King needs before the pawn can advance safely.

positions.prompt: White has a pawn on b2. Where should the King go?
positions.idea: Head toward the key squares (a4, b4, c4). Kd3 starts the march toward c4.
positions.on_correct: Good. Kd3 heads toward the key square c4. Once your King arrives there, the pawn promotes by force.
positions.on_wrong: b3 pushes the pawn too early. Your King needs to reach the key squares first.
positions.rule_reminder: Key squares for a pawn on the 2nd rank: three squares on the 4th rank. Get your King there.

positions.prompt: White to move. How do you secure the promotion?
positions.idea: Kd4 claims a key square (d4, e4, f4 are key squares for the e-pawn on e2). From d4, the pawn is unstoppable.
positions.on_correct: Kd4 occupies the key square. Black's King can't prevent promotion now.
positions.on_wrong: e4 pushes the pawn without controlling the key squares. The King must occupy them first.
positions.rule_reminder: Occupy the key square, then push the pawn. Not the other way around.

positions.prompt: White to move. The pawn is on c3. What's the winning plan?
positions.idea: Kd4 makes Black's King choose a side. White can then reach b5, c5, or d5 in front of the pawn.
positions.on_correct: Kd4 makes Black choose a side, and White's King can move into one of the target squares.
positions.on_wrong: c4 pushes the pawn but doesn't secure a key square. The King does the heavy lifting in endgames.
positions.rule_reminder: The King must claim key squares. The pawn just follows.

square_rule.name: Rule of the Square
square_rule.rule: Draw a mental square from the pawn to its promotion square. If the defending King can step inside that square, it catches the pawn.
square_rule.description: A quick visual trick to calculate if a King can catch a passed pawn without counting every move.

intro.headline: Draw the box. Step inside.
intro.body:
When a pawn is racing to promote and no piece defends it, imagine a square from the pawn to its promotion square. If your King can step INSIDE that box on its turn, the pawn is caught. If it can't, the pawn promotes.

A King's diagonal move counts the same as a straight move — that's why this works. Moving diagonally gets you closer to both the pawn's file AND the promotion rank at the same time.
intro.example_caption: Black's pawn is on b4 running to b1. The box is b4–b1–e1–e4. White's King on e1 is already inside the box — the pawn is caught.

positions.concept: The box is b5–f5–f1–b1 (the green circles). Your King is on g6 — outside the box, both file (g) and rank (6). Look for the ONE move that steps inside both dimensions.
positions.prompt: Which move enters the box?
positions.idea: The box is files b–f × ranks 1–5. From g6 the King can only reach f5 as a box square — Kf5 is the unique entering move. From there, the King races diagonally to catch the pawn.
positions.on_correct: Kf5 is the one square inside the box. The King now marches diagonally down-and-left (Ke4, Kd3, Kc2) and captures the pawn as it queens.
positions.on_wrong: That move stays outside the box — either wrong file OR wrong rank. Kf6 looks tempting (file f is inside) but rank 6 is outside the box, so the King still can't catch in time.
positions.rule_reminder: The box has TWO boundaries — file AND rank. A move inside one but outside the other is still outside.

positions.concept: The box is g4–g1–d1–d4 (files d–g, ranks 1–4). Your King is on c5 — one file west and one rank north of the box corner. Only one diagonal step lands you inside both boundaries.
positions.prompt: Which move enters the box?
positions.idea: From c5 only Kd4 lands on a file d–g AND a rank 1–4 square. Other moves either stay outside the file range (b-squares) or outside the rank range (d5, d6). Kd4 races diagonally to intercept the pawn before it promotes.
positions.on_correct: Kd4 is the one square inside the box. The King runs east-and-south (Ke3, Kf2) to catch the pawn at g1.
positions.on_wrong: Kd5 is a trap — the file d is inside the box, but the rank 5 is outside it. The pawn promotes untouched.
positions.rule_reminder: The box has TWO boundaries — file AND rank. One diagonal step can cross both at once, or neither.

positions.concept: The box is a4–a1–d1–d4 (files a–d, ranks 1–4). Your King is on e5 — one file east and one rank north of the box corner. Find the single move that steps inside both file and rank at once.
positions.prompt: Which move enters the box?
positions.idea: From e5 only Kd4 is inside the box (file d ≤ d, rank 4 ≤ 4). Other moves either stay on file e (outside) or on rank 5 (outside). Kd4 races diagonally to catch the a-pawn.
positions.on_correct: Kd4 is the one square inside the box. The King runs diagonally (Kc3, Kb2) to intercept the pawn at a1.
positions.on_wrong: Kd5 drops to the d-file but stays on rank 5 — outside the box. Tempting but wrong. The pawn promotes in 3 moves and you can't catch it from this distance.
positions.rule_reminder: The diagonal entering move is always the best — it crosses both the file AND the rank in one step.

breakthrough.name: Pawn Breakthrough
breakthrough.rule: Sacrifice a pawn to create a passed pawn that the enemy King can't stop.
breakthrough.description: When pawns face each other and Kings are far away, a well-timed sacrifice can create an unstoppable passer.

positions.prompt: The Kings are far away. How can White force one pawn through?
positions.idea: g6! offers the middle pawn. If the h-pawn captures it, f6 creates a runner. If the f-pawn captures it, h6 creates the runner instead.
positions.on_correct: g6 forces Black to choose which outside pawn White will free. The middle pawn is the key that opens one side.
positions.on_wrong: h6 lets Black answer ...gxh6 and keep the pawns under control. Offer the middle pawn with g6 first.
positions.rule_reminder: When three pawns face three pawns, test the middle-pawn offer. It can free either outside pawn.

positions.prompt: The same breakthrough appears on the other wing. Which pawn must move first?
positions.idea: b6! offers the middle pawn. After ...cxb6, a6! forces a pawn through; after ...axb6, c6! does the same job.
positions.on_correct: b6 makes one of the outside pawns impossible to stop. Calculate both captures before you play it.
positions.on_wrong: a6 closes one route and gives Black time. The middle-pawn offer with b6 is what opens a path.
positions.rule_reminder: Do not memorize a file. Recognize the shape: the middle pawn is sacrificed so an outside pawn can run.

positions.prompt: After g6 ...hxg6, which pawn completes the breakthrough?
positions.idea: f6! cannot be stopped by the g7-pawn: ...gxf6 lets h6 and h7 follow, while waiting lets f7 and f8=Q follow.
positions.on_correct: f6 is the second half of the combination. The pawn that was furthest from the capture becomes the runner.
positions.on_wrong: hxg6 removes a pawn but gives up the promotion race. The point of g6 was to free f6 immediately.
positions.rule_reminder: A breakthrough is a sequence, not one move: offer the middle pawn, then push the outside pawn that was freed.

king_centralization.name: King to the Center
king_centralization.rule: In the endgame, your King is a FIGHTING piece. Centralize it immediately.
king_centralization.description: The moment the Queens are off the board, your King transforms from a liability into your strongest piece. Get it to the center.

positions.prompt: Endgame. Both sides have pawns. What's White's first priority?
positions.idea: Centralize the King! Kf2 starts the march toward d3-e4. Pawn moves can wait — the King decides the endgame.
positions.on_correct: Kf2 begins centralization. Next: Ke3, then Kd3 or Ke4. The King will dominate the center.
positions.on_wrong: a3 wastes time on the flank. Your King is on g1 doing nothing — that's the real problem.
positions.rule_reminder: Queens are gone? King to the center. This is endgame rule #1.

positions.prompt: Locked pawn structure. How does White improve?
positions.idea: March the King toward the action. Kd2 heads for c3-b4 to attack Black's queenside or support a breakthrough.
positions.on_correct: Kd2 starts the King march. The plan is Kc3-Kb4 to attack the weak points in Black's position.
positions.on_wrong: Ke2 centralizes but aims at a less productive square. Kd2-Kc3-Kb4 targets Black's weakness.
positions.rule_reminder: Centralize with PURPOSE. Aim your King at the opponent's weaknesses.

positions.prompt: Pawn endgame. What should White do first?
positions.idea: Kf2 starts centralizing. Pushing g5 prematurely weakens the pawn. The King must be active first.
positions.on_correct: Kf2 first, then Ke3, Kd4. The centralized King will support BOTH flanks.
positions.on_wrong: g5 pushes a pawn without King support. In endgames, the King must be active before pawns advance.
positions.rule_reminder: King first, pawns second. A centralized King supports everything.

rook_endgames.name: Rook Endgames
rook_endgames.description: The most common endgame type. Master the Lucena, Philidor, and rook activity.

lucena.name: Shield the King from Checks (Lucena)
lucena.rule: Put your Rook on the fourth rank, move the King out, then use the Rook as a shield against checks.
lucena.description: When your pawn is one step from promotion and the enemy Rook checks from the side, build a shield: your Rook blocks the checks so the King can escape.

positions.prompt: White has K on b8, P on b7, R on h1. How do you win?
positions.idea: Rh4! places the rook on the 4th rank to later block Black's checks. This is the Bridge.
positions.on_correct: Rh4 prepares the bridge. Next: Kc7, and when Black checks from behind, Rb4 blocks everything.
positions.on_wrong: Rh8 doesn't help. You need the Rook on the 4th rank to build the bridge.
positions.rule_reminder: Step 1: Rook to the 4th rank. Step 2: King steps out. Step 3: Rook blocks the checks.

positions.prompt: Same idea, different placement. White to move.
positions.idea: Re4 goes to the 4th rank — the bridge position. From here, when the King steps out, the Rook will block checks.
positions.on_correct: Re4 is the bridge setup. Now Kc7, and Rc4 will block any checks from behind.
positions.on_wrong: Re8 doesn't set up the bridge. The 4th rank is the key.
positions.rule_reminder: The 4th rank. Always the 4th rank. That's where the bridge is built.

positions.prompt: The bridge is already set (Rook on e4). What now?
positions.idea: Step out with the King! Ke7 moves toward the Rook. When Black checks, Re5 or another block completes the bridge.
positions.on_correct: Ke7 is the next step. The Rook on e4 is ready to block checks. The pawn will promote.
positions.on_wrong: Kg8 moves the wrong direction. You need to step TOWARD the Rook to use the bridge.
positions.rule_reminder: Bridge built? King marches toward the Rook. The Rook blocks the checks.

philidor.name: Philidor — Third Rank Defense
philidor.rule: Keep your Rook on the 6th rank (3rd rank as Black). When the pawn reaches the 6th, switch to the back rank for infinite checks.
philidor.description: The drawing technique when defending Rook vs Rook + Pawn. Hold the 6th rank, then switch to checking from behind.

positions.prompt: Black's rook already blocks the White King from the side. What should Black do when a side check is available?
positions.idea: Ra5+ sends the King away from the pawn. The defender keeps checking from the side instead of waiting passively behind the pawn.
positions.on_correct: Ra5+ uses the rook's distance. White must move the King, so the e-pawn cannot advance with support.
positions.on_wrong: Ra8 gives up the useful side check and lets White improve. Check from the side while the King is exposed.
positions.rule_reminder: In the Philidor defense, deny the King shelter. Use side checks before switching behind the pawn.

positions.prompt: White's King stepped to e6. Should Black rush behind the pawn or keep checking from the side?
positions.idea: Ra6+ keeps the White King exposed. Moving to a1 now would let White escape the checks and turn the draw into a win.
positions.on_correct: Ra6+ is the only move that keeps the exact draw. The check forces the King to move before the pawn can advance.
positions.on_wrong: Ra8 stops checking and gives White time to coordinate the King and pawn. Keep using side checks while they work.
positions.rule_reminder: Do not switch behind the pawn by memory alone. Keep checking from the side until the attacker finds shelter.

positions.prompt: White's King is on f5, pawn on e6. Black to move.
positions.idea: Ra5+! drives the White King away from the pawn. If the King goes to e-file to support the pawn, Black takes. If King hides, Ra1 and check from behind.
positions.on_correct: Ra5+ is precise. It forces the King to choose: leave the pawn or go in front of it (blocking promotion).
positions.on_wrong: Rxe6 trades into a King vs King draw — but why give up the Rook? You had a clean defense with checks.
positions.rule_reminder: Checks from behind are the defender's best friend. The attacker's King can't advance AND support the pawn.

active_rook.name: Rook Activity
active_rook.rule: An active Rook is worth more than a pawn. Never trap your Rook in a passive defense.
active_rook.description: In rook endgames, the activity of your Rook matters more than material. A Rook on the 7th rank or behind a passed pawn dominates.

positions.prompt: White must hold this rook endgame. Which move checks from a safe distance?
positions.idea: Ra8+ checks along the back rank while keeping the rook far from Black's king and rook. The active check preserves the draw.
positions.on_correct: Ra8+ makes Black answer the check. White keeps enough activity to hold the game.
positions.on_wrong: Rh7 stops checking and places the rook where Black can coordinate an attack. Keep checking from the side or behind.
positions.rule_reminder: When defending a rook endgame, active checks can be worth more than guarding a pawn.

positions.prompt: White is a pawn up. How can the rook improve with a threat?
positions.idea: Re1+ moves the rook to an open file with check. Black's king must move before it can attack White's pawns.
positions.on_correct: Re1+ improves the rook and gains a move by checking the king.
positions.on_wrong: Ra3 moves the rook without creating a threat. Use the open rank to check from the side.
positions.rule_reminder: Improve the rook with a check when the check also gives it a useful file or rank.

positions.prompt: White has a passed b5-pawn. Where should the pieces go?
positions.idea: Ka4 supports the pawn advance. The Rook on b1 is already behind the passed pawn (perfect!). Now the King supports b6.
positions.on_correct: Ka4 supports b6 next. With the Rook behind the pawn, this is textbook technique.
positions.on_wrong: Rb2 doesn't accomplish anything. The Rook is already perfectly placed behind the passed pawn.
positions.rule_reminder: Rooks belong BEHIND passed pawns. Both yours AND your opponent's.

queen_vs_pawn.name: Queen vs Pawn
queen_vs_pawn.description: Queen vs advanced pawn. Win by stopping promotion, and watch for stalemate traps.

stop_promotion.name: Stopping Promotion
stop_promotion.rule: Stop the pawn with a pin, block, or useful check, then bring your King closer while the Queen keeps control.
stop_promotion.description: A Queen stops a dangerous pawn by controlling its next square. Once the pawn cannot move, bring the King closer and repeat.

positions.prompt: Black has the Queen. How do you freeze the b-pawn before bringing the King closer?
positions.idea: Qb4 pins the b-pawn to the King on b1. The pawn cannot move because exposing the King would be illegal.
positions.on_correct: Qb4 freezes the pawn. Black can now walk the King closer without allowing promotion.
positions.on_wrong: Qc3 looks active, but it gives up the exact win. Pin the pawn from b4 so it cannot move at all.
positions.rule_reminder: If the pawn is pinned to its King, stop checking and bring your King closer.

positions.prompt: The a-pawn is about to promote. Black's Queen must act.
positions.idea: Qd1+ checks the King. After Ka2 (forced into front of pawn), bring your King closer while the pawn is blocked.
positions.on_correct: Qd1+ forces the King to block its own pawn. Classic technique.
positions.on_wrong: Qa3 pins but doesn't solve the problem long-term. The check-approach method is the winning technique.
positions.rule_reminder: Give check from the direction that forces the King IN FRONT of the pawn.

positions.prompt: White's d-pawn wants to advance. Which queen move blocks it and keeps the win?
positions.idea: Qd3 places the Queen directly in front of the pawn. The pawn cannot advance, so Black's King has time to approach.
positions.on_correct: Qd3 blockades the pawn. Now the King can come closer without a promotion race.
positions.on_wrong: Qc3+ is a check, but exact tablebase play says it throws away the win. A useful block is better than a check with no lasting control.
positions.rule_reminder: Not every check helps. First make sure the pawn's next square stays controlled.

stalemate_tricks.name: Stalemate Traps
stalemate_tricks.rule: Watch out! Some pawns on the 7th rank create stalemate if the King reaches the corner. Bishop-pawn and rook-pawn are the tricky ones.
stalemate_tricks.description: Not all Queen vs pawn positions are wins. Learn when stalemate lurks and how to avoid or exploit it.

positions.prompt: White has an f-pawn on f2. Black has a Queen. Be careful — is there a stalemate trap?
positions.idea: Qf3 controls the pawn's next square and keeps the White King boxed in without taking away every legal move.
positions.on_correct: Qf3 keeps the win and avoids an accidental stalemate. Now Black can bring the King closer before taking the pawn.
positions.on_wrong: Ke3 walks into the pawn's path. Keep the Queen active first, then approach with the King.
positions.rule_reminder: Central and bishop/knight pawns are normal wins. Rook-pawn (a/h) is the stalemate danger zone.

positions.prompt: White's a-pawn is on the 7th! King is in the corner. Can Black win?
positions.idea: Qf8+ keeps White's King moving. The position is drawn with correct defense because taking the a-pawn can leave the King with no legal move.
positions.on_correct: Qf8+ avoids stalemate for this move, but it does not create a win. The lesson is to recognize that the corner King and rook-pawn can hold the draw.
positions.on_wrong: Qb7 is stalemate immediately! The King has no squares — that's exactly the trap.
positions.rule_reminder: Queen vs rook-pawn (a or h file) with King in the corner = DRAW. This is one of the most important things to know.

positions.prompt: d-pawn on d2. Normal pawn, no stalemate worries. What's the technique?
positions.idea: Qa5 controls the d-file and approaches. The d-pawn (center pawn) has no stalemate tricks. Standard check-approach pattern wins.
positions.on_correct: Qa5 controls the key squares. Next, approach with your King. Center pawns are always a clean win.
positions.on_wrong: Qd5 blocks the d-file but your King is too far. Qa5 lets you approach while maintaining control.
positions.rule_reminder: Center pawns and knight/bishop pawns = clean wins for the Queen. Only rook-pawns (a/h) are tricky.

bishop_endgames.name: Bishop Endgames
bishop_endgames.description: Good bishop vs bad bishop, opposite-color draws, and when bishops beat knights.

good_vs_bad_bishop.name: Good Bishop vs Bad Bishop
good_vs_bad_bishop.rule: A bishop blocked by its own pawns is BAD. Put your pawns on the OPPOSITE color of your bishop.
good_vs_bad_bishop.description: Your bishop is 'good' when your pawns are on the opposite color squares, giving it open diagonals. A 'bad' bishop is trapped behind its own pawns.

positions.prompt: White has a light-squared bishop. Pawns are on dark squares. Is this bishop good or bad?
positions.idea: This is a GOOD bishop — pawns on d4, e5, f4 (dark) leave the light diagonals open. Bd3 aims at the kingside.
positions.on_correct: Bd3 activates the good bishop. It eyes f5 and h7. Your pawns don't block your bishop — that's the key.
positions.on_wrong: Bd1 retreats the bishop to a passive square. Use the open diagonals — that's why it's a good bishop.
positions.rule_reminder: Pawns on dark squares + light-squared bishop = GOOD. The bishop has open highways.

positions.prompt: Black's bishop on d7 is blocked by the pawn on c6. How can Black open a useful diagonal?
positions.idea: c5 moves the c-pawn off c6 and opens d7-c6-b5-a4 for the bishop. Improve the blocked bishop by moving the pawn that cages it.
positions.on_correct: c5 gives the bishop a route to b5 and a4. The bishop becomes useful because one blocking pawn moved away.
positions.on_wrong: Ke8 leaves the bishop trapped behind c6. Fix the piece that has no route before making a waiting King move.
positions.rule_reminder: If your bishop is blocked by your own pawns, move one blocking pawn to open a diagonal.

positions.prompt: Both sides have bishops. Compare them. Which side stands better?
positions.idea: White's bishop on e3 is GOOD (pawns on light squares a2, b5, c4, e4). Black's bishop on e6 is BAD (pawns on dark squares block nothing, but bishop has no targets). Activate the King.
positions.on_correct: Kf2 starts centralizing. White's good bishop + active King will dominate Black's bad bishop.
positions.on_wrong: a4 pushes a pawn but doesn't address the real advantage: King activity combined with the better bishop.
positions.rule_reminder: Good bishop + active King = winning formula. Bad bishop + passive King = suffering.

opposite_color_bishops.name: Opposite-Color Bishop Draws
opposite_color_bishops.rule: Opposite-color bishops favor the DEFENDER. Even 2 pawns up can be a draw because the bishops can never interact.
opposite_color_bishops.description: When each side has a bishop on a different color, the defender can set up a fortress. The attacker's bishop can't challenge the defender's blockade.

positions.prompt: Black is 2 pawns up but the bishops are on opposite colors. Can White hold?
positions.idea: Bxc1 removes Black's bishop before setting up the blockade. With only the two pawns left, White's King and bishop can hold them.
positions.on_correct: Bxc1 trades the piece that could support the pawns. The remaining pawn ending is held with a blockade.
positions.on_wrong: Bd2 is passive. Bc5 sets up the blockade on the right diagonal. The key is blocking the passed pawns on squares your bishop controls.
positions.rule_reminder: Opposite-color bishops = drawing weapon. Blockade the pawns on YOUR bishop's color.

positions.prompt: Equal material, opposite-color bishops. What's the best strategy?
positions.idea: e5+ fixes Black's pawns and forces the King to respond. White keeps the position level by preventing Black from creating a protected runner.
positions.on_correct: e5+ closes the route for Black's King and keeps the draw. The check gives White the time needed to hold the pawns.
positions.on_wrong: Bg4 lets Black improve the King and can turn the draw into a loss. Use the forcing pawn check now.
positions.rule_reminder: Opposite-color bishops often draw, but only if you stop the King and pawns before they cross your blockade.

positions.prompt: White has a passed b-pawn. Can the opposite-color bishops help or hurt?
positions.idea: Bxf4 removes Black's bishop. Once the defender's bishop disappears, the b-pawn can advance without being attacked from f4.
positions.on_correct: Bxf4 wins the defending bishop and leaves White with a simple passed-pawn win.
positions.on_wrong: Ke2 misses the free bishop on f4. Before planning a pawn race, check whether you can remove the defender immediately.
positions.rule_reminder: The drawing power of opposite-color bishops disappears if one bishop can be captured. Check captures first.

knight_endgames.name: Knight Endgames
knight_endgames.description: Knights love closed positions, outposts, and blockading pawns. Master knight technique.

knight_vs_bishop.name: Knight vs Bishop
knight_vs_bishop.rule: Knights love CLOSED positions with fixed pawns. Bishops love OPEN positions with pawns on both sides.
knight_vs_bishop.description: The eternal debate. In closed positions with pawns locked on one color, the knight dominates. In open positions, the bishop's range wins.

positions.prompt: Closed position. Knight vs no bishop. How does the knight dominate?
positions.idea: Ne3! heads for d5 or f5 — powerful outposts. In closed positions, the knight hops over pawns while a bishop would be blocked.
positions.on_correct: Ne3 starts the knight journey to an outpost on d5 or f5. Knights thrive in closed positions — they jump over the pawn chains.
positions.on_wrong: Nb2 heads to the wrong side. The knight needs to reach a central outpost like d5 or f5.
positions.rule_reminder: Closed position = knight is better. It hops over locked pawns that would block a bishop.

positions.prompt: Knight vs knight endgame. Pawns are locked. What matters most?
positions.idea: Nc5! grabs the outpost. In knight endgames, OUTPOSTS are everything. The knight on c5 dominates — it attacks a7, b7, d7, e6.
positions.on_correct: Nc5 is a dominant outpost. The knight controls key squares and can't be challenged. Knight endgames are about outposts.
positions.on_wrong: Kd2 retreats the King. The knight needs to occupy the outpost FIRST — then the King supports.
positions.rule_reminder: Knight endgames = find the outpost. A centralized knight on an outpost is worth almost a rook.

positions.prompt: The knight can go to f3, aiming for g5-e6, or b5, aiming at the queenside. Which plan?
positions.idea: Nf3! heads for g5 or h4, targeting the kingside. The knight reroutes to attack weaknesses the opponent can't easily defend.
positions.on_correct: Nf3 reroutes to g5, attacking e6 and h7. Knights can change direction quickly — that's their superpower.
positions.on_wrong: Nb5 reaches an outpost but has no targets. The kingside offers real weaknesses to attack.
positions.rule_reminder: Knights reroute easily. Don't settle for a pretty square — aim for one that attacks real weaknesses.

knight_blockade.name: Knight Blockade
knight_blockade.rule: A knight is the BEST blockader. It blocks a passed pawn while remaining active — unlike a bishop or rook.
knight_blockade.description: When blocking a passed pawn, the knight doesn't lose any strength. It sits in front of the pawn AND controls squares around it.

positions.prompt: White has a passed b5-pawn. How does the knight blockade?
positions.idea: Nd7! prepares to blockade on b6 after ...Nb6. The knight on b6 stops the pawn AND controls a4, c4, d5, d7, a8, c8.
positions.on_correct: Nd7 heading to b6 is the perfect blockade. The knight stops the pawn while radiating power in all directions.
positions.on_wrong: Nc8 blockades but from a terrible square. On c8 the knight is passive. On b6 it's active AND blocking.
positions.rule_reminder: Knights are the ideal blockaders. They lose ZERO strength when sitting in front of a pawn.

positions.prompt: Black has a passed d5-pawn. Set up the knight blockade.
positions.idea: Nd3! blockades on d4 next move. The knight on d4 will stop the pawn while controlling b3, b5, c6, e6, f5, f3, c2, e2.
positions.on_correct: Nd3 prepares the perfect blockade square d4. The knight will be a monster there — blocking AND attacking.
positions.on_wrong: Kd4 blocks with the King, but the King could be doing other things. Let the knight blockade — it's designed for this job.
positions.rule_reminder: Use the knight to blockade, free the King for other tasks. The knight doesn't mind blocking.

positions.prompt: White's c-pawn is on c6 — dangerous! Black's knight must act immediately.
positions.idea: Nb5! blockades the pawn on c7 while attacking it. The knight controls the promotion square AND attacks the pawn.
positions.on_correct: Nb5 is perfect — the knight covers c7 (promotion square) and can take the pawn. That's the ideal blockade.
positions.on_wrong: Ne6 blocks c7 but is less flexible. Nb5 directly attacks the pawn and controls both a7 and c7.
positions.rule_reminder: Blockade on the square IN FRONT of the pawn. The knight covers the promotion square and remains active.

practical_endgames.name: Practical Endgame Skills
practical_endgames.description: Essential techniques every player needs: converting advantages, creating passed pawns, and using Zugzwang.

creating_passed_pawn.name: Creating a Passed Pawn
creating_passed_pawn.rule: A passed pawn is a pawn with no enemy pawn blocking or guarding its path. Create one — it's a winning weapon.
creating_passed_pawn.description: The most important endgame skill: create a passed pawn and escort it to promotion. The opponent's pieces get tied down defending.

positions.prompt: How does White create a passed pawn?
positions.idea: axb5! creates a passed a-pawn (or b-pawn after ...axb4). The recapture creates a pawn with a clear path to promotion.
positions.on_correct: axb5 creates a passed pawn. Now it's a race — push the passer while the opponent's King chases it.
positions.on_wrong: b4 locks the pawns. No passed pawn is created. You need to EXCHANGE to create a passer.
positions.rule_reminder: To create a passed pawn: exchange a pawn to leave one with a clear path. Don't lock the structure.

positions.prompt: White has two pawns against Black's a-pawn. How can White force a passed pawn?
positions.idea: b5! offers the b-pawn. If ...axb5, then axb5 leaves White with a passed b-pawn and a clear route to promotion.
positions.on_correct: b5 forces the only black pawn to leave the a-file. White recaptures and creates a passed pawn.
positions.on_wrong: a5 lets Black block with ...b5 no longer available as a capture idea. Use b5 to force the exchange on your terms.
positions.rule_reminder: Create a passed pawn by forcing the enemy pawn to capture, then recapture onto the newly opened file.

positions.prompt: White has two pawns against Black's g-pawn. Which pawn creates the runner?
positions.idea: f5! offers the f-pawn. If ...gxf5, then gxf5 creates a passed f-pawn. If Black waits, f6 becomes dangerous by itself.
positions.on_correct: f5 creates a passed pawn whichever way Black reacts. The neighboring pawn is ready to recapture.
positions.on_wrong: g5 locks the pawns and removes the useful capture. Offer the f-pawn so g4 can recapture onto an open file.
positions.rule_reminder: The pawn beside the enemy pawn often makes the break; its neighbor recaptures and becomes the passer.

zugzwang.name: Make Them Move (Zugzwang)
zugzwang.rule: Zugzwang means every available move makes the position worse. Use a waiting route so your opponent has to move first.
zugzwang.description: Sometimes the position would be safe if a player could pass. Chess has no pass, so use your King to lose a turn and make the opponent step away.

positions.prompt: The position is locked. White needs to give Black the move. How?
positions.idea: Kc3 starts a three-step waiting route: Kc3, Kd3, Kd4. Black runs out of safe waiting moves and must step away.
positions.on_correct: Kc3 begins the waiting route. White returns to d4 only after making Black move first.
positions.on_wrong: Ke3 moves away from the useful squares. Stay close and take the longer King route so Black must move first.
positions.rule_reminder: When moving first would hurt you, take a safe King route that returns to the same job after the opponent has moved.

positions.prompt: Classic Zugzwang setup. White to move. How do you win?
positions.idea: Kf6 leaves Black with no useful waiting move. After ...Ke8, Ke6 makes the King step away from the f7-pawn.
positions.on_correct: Kf6 creates the setup. After ...Ke8 and Ke6, every Black move gives up ground.
positions.on_wrong: f6 lets Black hold the draw after ...Ke8. The King must lead the pawn.
positions.rule_reminder: When your opponent has no safe move, keep the pawn back and make their King move first.

positions.prompt: How does White create Zugzwang?
positions.idea: Kf2 starts the long route Ke3, Kd3, Kc4, Kb5. White approaches from the other side until Black's King cannot guard both wings.
positions.on_correct: Kf2 begins the long route around. Black's King cannot hold both sides forever.
positions.on_wrong: gxf5+ opens the position but simplifies. Keep the tension — the locked structure is what creates Zugzwang.
positions.rule_reminder: Keep the pawns locked while your King changes sides. Make the defending King choose what it can no longer guard.

outside_passed_pawn.name: Outside Passed Pawn
outside_passed_pawn.rule: An outside passed pawn wins because it decoys the enemy King away from the main action.
outside_passed_pawn.description: The outside passed pawn is a decoy. Push it, force the opponent's King to chase it, then your King eats the undefended pawns on the other side.

positions.prompt: White has an outside passed a-pawn. What's the winning plan?
positions.idea: a4! starts pushing the outside passer. Black's King must chase it, leaving the kingside pawns undefended. Then White's King eats them.
positions.on_correct: a4 starts the decoy operation. The a-pawn runs, Black's King chases, White's King feasts on the kingside. Classic technique.
positions.on_wrong: Kf3 is too slow. Push the a-pawn NOW — it's a decoy that wins the game by distraction.
positions.rule_reminder: Outside passed pawn = decoy. Push it, force the King to chase, clean up the other side.

positions.prompt: White's a-pawn is the outside passer. Black's King guards the kingside. What's the plan?
positions.idea: a4! pushes the decoy. After a4-a5-a6, Black's King must come to the queenside. Then Kxe5 and Kf6 wins the g6-pawn too.
positions.on_correct: a4 is the start. The a-pawn marches, Black's King leaves the kingside, and White cleans up. Textbook.
positions.on_wrong: Kd5 moves toward the e-pawn but doesn't use the outside passer advantage. The a-pawn is your winning weapon — use it.
positions.rule_reminder: The outside passer doesn't need to promote. It just needs to pull the King away.

positions.prompt: Both sides have an a-pawn and g-pawn, but White's a-pawn is more advanced. How does this help?
positions.idea: a5! advances the pawn. It's further from the kingside than Black's a7-pawn, so Black's King must travel further to stop it. White wins the foot race.
positions.on_correct: a5 gains a full move in the pawn race. White's passer is further advanced, so Black's King cannot handle both sides.
positions.on_wrong: Ke4 gives away that extra move. The outside passer must advance now before Black can set up a defense.
positions.rule_reminder: More advanced outside passer = bigger decoy range = more time for your King to win on the other side.

two_vs_one.name: Two Pawns vs One
two_vs_one.rule: Two connected pawns vs one pawn usually wins. Push the pawn that ISN'T blocked.
two_vs_one.description: The most common practical endgame: you have 2 pawns vs 1 on one side. The technique is simple but many players get it wrong.

positions.prompt: White has g4 and f2 vs Black's f4. How to win?
positions.idea: Kxf4 removes Black's last pawn while keeping both White pawns. White then has two connected pawns and an active King against a lone King.
positions.on_correct: Kxf4 is the cleanest win: remove Black's only pawn first, then walk the connected pawns forward with the King.
positions.on_wrong: g5+ leaves Black's f-pawn alive and turns the position into a race. Capture it now while the King can do so safely.
positions.rule_reminder: Before starting a pawn race, check whether your King can remove the opponent's last pawn for free.

positions.prompt: White has f4 and g4 vs Black's g5. Find the winning move.
positions.idea: f5+! advances the unblocked pawn. The g4-pawn supports. If ...Kf6, g5+ continues the advance. The pawns support each other.
positions.on_correct: f5+ is correct. The connected pawns roll forward together — one advances, the other supports. Unstoppable.
positions.on_wrong: fxg5 trades into one pawn vs zero — drawable if Black's King reaches the right squares. Keep BOTH pawns.
positions.rule_reminder: Never trade down to one pawn when you can keep two. Two connected pawns rolling forward is almost always winning.

positions.prompt: White has f3 and g3 vs nothing. Simple — but which pawn goes first?
positions.idea: f4! advances with King support. The plan: f4-f5, then g4-g5, rolling forward together. The King on e3 supports the f-pawn.
positions.on_correct: f4 advances the pawn closest to King support. The connected pawns will march forward in tandem.
positions.on_wrong: g4 advances the wrong pawn. The f-pawn has King support — push the supported pawn first.
positions.rule_reminder: Push the pawn your King supports. Connected pawns advance in tandem — one at a time, supporting each other.
